title: Strayhorn's work habits compared with Duke's
summary: Duke wrote continually; Strayhorn wrote only on assignment and liked to party and jam.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Yeah. Incidentally, you know, it's interesting, but after Stray came with the band, you know, and Duke, you know, brought him on and brought him along and everything, you know, and then was so happy to find that they could dovetail in and Stray could pick up from him and so on, but the -- I've heard this, and I hadn't heard it at the time, but I believe this is true, that one of the big differences between them was that Duke wrote all the time. And Strayhorn didn't write all the time, by any manner of means. He wrote any time Duke put him on a project. And he had to be prodded, too, remember, like Duke, too, he had to be pushed to get it done in time, etcetera, etcetera, you know. But Duke used to, you know, maybe leave him behind when they went on the road and tell him,
"Work on this or that," or whatever. But I mean, Stray was not like Duke, in that, Duke, like you say, always wrote.
Yeah.
You'd get off at night, you'd finish at the theater, and he always wrote, didn't he?
That's right.
And he'd go where the room was, where there was a piano.
Yes.
And he'd write. But, I think that must have been one of the huge differences, was that Duke was so tremendously prolific.
Oh, yeah.

You know, but I mean, a lot of people I think thought, when it first became such a marvel, you know, that these two guys could interchange, or pick up where one left off and carry on, and that you wouldn't be able to recognize the difference in style. You know, I think a lot of people thought that maybe Strayhorn was turning out an awful lot of the things. But the difference between them -- well, I think, you know, Strayhorn liked to ball, too, didn't he? He liked to get out and have a good time.
Yeah.
Yeah. I think I'm right on that, Cootie, am I? Or am I putting words in your mouth?

No, no. You're absolutely right. Strayhorn was a young boy, you know. He wasn't no stay in like Duke, and sit at no piano all day and all night, just continuously, day in and day out, you know, like that. No. He wasn't going to do that. He used to like to party and ball.
Yeah. Yeah.
You know.

Can you remember -- I can remember when he first came. I remember the first trip he took in the bus. I mean, he was such a little guy, and it was a funny thing for him to fall in that band and fall on his feet and everything, right?
Oh, yeah. Yeah. I recall when I used to go out with him, sometimes, we'd stay up all night, jamming.
Really?
Uh-huh.
No kidding. Where would you go?
One time we was in the Elks' Home, playing.
(Laughter)
Where? In New York?
No. That was out around St. Paul-Minneapolis, one of the towns. He set up all night playing.
No kidding. He loved to play, too, then,
Yeah. He loved to play then. And I loved to play then, too.
